heading_ja: 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in simple-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビ以外のルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: § A.22 has no table. Its whole body is the quoted sentence, once per locale, so cl-22 enumerates no code point and no code-point sequence and no case in this file puts a character in the class by key. What puts an occurrence in it is § 3.3.7's closing Note, the one sentence in the document that assigns a construct to a class: 'The complexes of base characters with ruby characters are classified as simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) and jukugo-ruby character complex (cl-23).' Membership is therefore a property of the complex the occurrence sits in, and the input states that complex rather than describing the character. Which distribution methods the class covers is fixed by § B.2 note 10 and by nothing else: it hands two adjacent characters of one cl-22 run to § 3.3.5 (mono-ruby) or § 3.3.6 (group-ruby) and names no third section, so cl-22 is mono-ruby together with group-ruby. This case is the mono-ruby half — Terminology defines mono-ruby as 'A method of ruby distribution where a run of ruby text is attached to each base character. (JIS Z 8125)', which is what the two `runs` below say. The base character is a CJK Unified Ideograph and would be cl-19 outside a complex; the companion case A.22/no-ruby/is-not-in-the-complex declares the same two characters with no ruby and answers cl-19, and the ruby construct is the only difference between the two inputs.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.22, with § 3.3.7's Note as the assignment)

forbidden.why: Classifying the base character by its key and ignoring the complex it sits in. U+6F22 is a CJK Unified Ideograph and § A.19's own sentence — 'The following is the list of all non-ideographic characters assigned to this character class' — makes it cl-19 when it stands alone. Answering cl-19 here indexes Appendix B's ideographic row and column for a base character that carries ruby, which makes § B.2 note 10, § C.2 note 7 and § E.2 note 6 unreachable: all three are stated for cl-22 and for nothing else.

cases.quote: When two adjacent characters belong to the same simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) run, set them according to the method explained in § 3.3.5 Positioning of Mono-ruby with Respect to Base Characters or § 3.3.6 Positioning of Group-ruby with Respect to Base Characters . When two adjacent characters belong to two distinct simple-ruby character complex runs, set them solid.
cases.rationale: The other half of the class, and the quoted note is the sentence that puts it there. Neither § A.22 nor § 3.9.2 says which methods of ruby distribution cl-22 covers — § A.22 says only that any character may participate and § 3.9.2's entry carries no prose at all beyond a Note reporting the JIS X 4051 class name — so the routing in § B.2 note 10 is the whole of the answer, and it routes to § 3.3.5 and § 3.3.6 and to no other section. Group-ruby is Terminology's 'method of ruby character distribution such that the length of ruby text matches to that of the base text by giving the same adjusted amount of space between ruby characters', which is one run of ruby text over a run of base characters, so the single `run` below covers both base characters and both are in one complex. The class is the same one the mono-ruby case answers: cl-22 does not record which of the two methods produced it, and an implementation that has two classes here has invented one. The three ruby characters against two base characters is § 3.3.6's unequal case and is a placement question, not a classification one; nothing below asserts a placement.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.22, with § B.2 note 10's routing)

forbidden.why: The same failure as in the mono-ruby case, reached from the other distribution method: U+5B50 is a Unified Ideograph and is cl-19 only while it is not a base character of a complex carrying ruby.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in simple-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビ以外のルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: Appendix A's Remarks column is where one key is separated into two classes by the frame (字幅) the caller measured it on, and U+0035 is the sharpest instance: § A.19 lists it with an empty Remark, § A.24 with 'half-width / 字幅は半角' and § A.27 with 'proportionally-spaced / プロポーショナル'. cl-22 has no table, so it has no Remarks cell and can draw no such line, and § A.22's sentence puts no condition on the key and none on the frame. A European numeral declared on the half-em frame is therefore cl-22 once it is a base character carrying ruby, exactly as an ideograph is. This case and its full-em and proportional twins differ in the declared frame and in the advance the caller measured and in nothing else, and their expectations are byte-identical; that equality is the assertion. An implementation that keeps the frame in play after the construct has decided the class answers cl-24 here, cl-19 on the full em and cl-27 on the proportional frame — three different classes for one occurrence that the document gives one.

forbidden.why: § A.24's Remark 'half-width / 字幅は半角' is what selects grouped numerals (cl-24) for a half-width U+0035, and cl-24 is itself a construct class — its heading is 'Grouped numerals (連数字中の文字)'. This input declares no grouped numeral and declares a ruby complex, so the construct that decides the class is the ruby one. Answering cl-24 reads a Remarks cell that belongs to a different class's table as though it qualified this occurrence.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in simple-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビ以外のルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: The middle of the three frames, and the one that completes the assertion. § A.19 lists U+0035 too, with an empty Remarks cell, and prints it as the full-width ５; so the same key reaches ideographic characters (cl-19) on the ideographic frame, grouped numerals (cl-24) on the half-em frame and Western characters (cl-27) on the proportional one, and Appendix A's Remarks column is the whole of what separates the three. cl-22 has no table and therefore no Remarks cell, and § A.22's sentence conditions nothing on the key or on the frame it was measured on. Every value in the expectation below is byte-identical to the half-em and proportional cases, and the three inputs differ only in `frame` and in the caller's own advance.

forbidden.why: § A.19 lists U+0035 with an empty Remarks cell, which is the reading a caller declares by measuring the key on the ideographic frame. It is still the reading of an occurrence standing in running text; this one is a base character of a complex carrying ruby, and § 3.3.7's Note classifies such complexes without reference to what their base characters would otherwise be.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in simple-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビ以外のルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: The third frame, with the same numeral declared proportionally — the advance a Western font reports for the same key — and the same ruby over it. § A.27 lists U+0035 as 'proportionally-spaced / プロポーショナル' and that Remark is what makes a bare occurrence Western characters (cl-27), so a classifier that consults the frame after the construct has spoken answers differently here than in the other two cases. It must not: § A.22 states no frame, has no Remarks column in which to state one, and admits any character. Every value in the expectation below is byte-identical to the half-em and full-em cases, and the three inputs differ only in `frame` and in the caller's own advance.

forbidden.why: § A.27's Remark 'proportionally-spaced / プロポーショナル' selects Western characters (cl-27) for a proportionally measured U+0035 that stands in running text. This occurrence does not stand in running text: it is a base character of a complex carrying ruby, and § 3.3.7's Note classifies such complexes as cl-22 or cl-23 without reference to what the base characters would otherwise be.

cases.quote: The complexes of base characters with ruby characters are classified as simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) and jukugo-ruby character complex (cl-23). The handling and positioning of these complexes with adjacent characters is discussed in § B. Spacing between Characters as a complete table in accordance with § 3.9 About Character Classes.
cases.rationale: The boundary the document draws around this class, stated from the outside. The quoted Note assigns a class to a complex of base characters *with ruby characters*; where there is no ruby there is no complex, and nothing for an occurrence to be a member of. This input is A.22/mono-ruby-base/is-in-the-complex with the ruby construct removed and with `constructs` written out empty so the absence is a declaration rather than an omission, and the answer moves from cl-22 to cl-19. Read the negative carefully: it is not a statement about U+6F22. § A.22 admits every character without exception, so no code point is excluded from cl-22 and no case may claim one is; what excludes this occurrence is that the input declares no complex. cl-19 is the answer for the positive reason § A.19 gives in its own heading sentence — 'The following is the list of all non-ideographic characters assigned to this character class' — which makes that table the class's complement, so a Unified Ideograph is cl-19 without appearing in it.

forbidden.why: Reading § A.22's 'Any character may participate in simple-ruby character complex' as a membership statement rather than as a permission. Under that reading every character in every text is cl-22 and the class is universal, which contradicts § 3.9.2's own thirty-way partition and would make § B.2 note 10 apply to every adjacency in Japanese text. The sentence that assigns an occurrence to cl-22 is § 3.3.7's Note, and what it assigns is a complex.

cases.quote: EN: The name of this class in JIS X 4051 is "Characters included in base characters complex with ruby (excluding jukugo-ruby)". — JA: JIS X 4051の名称は，“熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き親文字群中の文字”である．
cases.rationale: The other boundary, and the sharpest input in this file: it is byte-identical to A.22/mono-ruby-base/is-in-the-complex except for one string, `style`, which reads 'jukugo' instead of 'mono'. The answer moves from cl-22 to cl-23. § A.22's Japanese name carries the condition — 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）, the characters of a base-character complex carrying ruby *other than* jukugo-ruby — and the quoted Note is the only place the English states it at all, as JIS X 4051's '(excluding jukugo-ruby)'. The English body of § A.22 states no condition: it says 'simple-ruby', a term the document's Terminology section never defines, defining mono-ruby, group-ruby, jukugo-ruby, general-ruby, para-ruby, one-third-ruby and furikanji and no simple-ruby. So this case takes the Japanese reading, and an implementation that reads only the English half has nothing to separate the two classes with. Note what cannot do the separating: `runs`. Mono-ruby and jukugo-ruby both pair one run of ruby text per base character — § 3.3.5 against § 3.3.7's opening sentence, which composes each run of a jukugo's ruby 'as described in § 3.3.5' when a kanji takes two ruby characters or fewer — so the two inputs below and above have the same runs. `style` is the only datum that names which class a ruby construct is, and the schema makes it optional; a ruby construct written without it names neither cl-22 nor cl-23, and every case in this file declares it.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2's Note for cl-22 read against its Note for cl-23, with § 3.3.7's Note as the split)

forbidden.why: cl-22 is the complexes carrying ruby other than jukugo-ruby, and this one carries jukugo-ruby. The two classes take different answers at every layer that reads them — § B.2 note 10 against note 11, § C.2 note 7 against note 8, § E.2 note 6 against note 7 — and § C.2 note 8 in particular opens a break between two base characters of one jukugo complex where § C.2 note 7 denies one inside a simple-ruby complex, so the confusion is observable in the line breaking and not only in the class.

cases.quote: EN: In principle, ruby is attached to the right of base characters in vertical writing mode, and above in horizontal writing mode. — JA: 縦組の場合，ルビは親文字の右側，横組の場合，ルビは親文字の上側に付けるのが原則である．
cases.rationale: cl-22 has no direction-conditional membership, and this case and its horizontal twin say so at the one place it would be easiest to acquire one. Everything else about a ruby complex does depend on the writing mode: the quoted § 3.3.4 puts the annotation on a different side in each mode from a single rule, and § 3.3.5 makes katatsuki (肩付き) top-alignment a vertical option and says 'for horizontal writing mode, katatsuki should not be adopted' — one of the three direction-conditional rules ADR 0011 names, and one with no reader in this workspace yet. None of that touches the class. § A.22 states no direction, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-22 carries no prose but the JIS X 4051 name, and no Remarks cell exists to carry a 縦組 or 横組 qualification because there is no table. So this case and A.22/simple-ruby-complex/horizontal-writing are byte-identical but for the declared direction, and their answers are byte-identical too. The direction is declared rather than left out on purpose: a case that leaves it out is composed both ways by the direction-parity gate, which proves the same thing for composition from M1; these two prove it for classification now, where that gate does not reach.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.22; § 3.3.4 and § 3.3.5 for what the direction does change)

cases.quote: EN: In vertical writing mode, attach a ruby character so that the top of its virtual body is aligned with the top of that of the base character ... This positioning of a ruby character is called 'katatsuki' (top-alignment). For horizontal writing mode, 'katatsuki' should not be adopted. — JA: 縦組においては親文字の上端とルビ文字の上端をそろえて配置する……なお，横組では，肩付きの配置方法にはしない．
cases.rationale: The horizontal twin. The quoted § 3.3.5 sentence is the strongest reason to expect a direction to reach the class here and the reason the pair is worth publishing: it forbids in horizontal writing an alignment it prescribes in vertical, for the very construct this class is about, and § B.2 note 10 routes same-complex cl-22 adjacency to that section. A rule about how a ruby character is aligned against its base is still not a rule about which class the base character is in, and cl-22 has no table and no Remarks cell in which a writing-mode qualification could be written. The expectation is byte-identical to the vertical case, and the two inputs differ in the single string `direction`.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.22; § 3.3.5 for what the direction does change)

cases.quote: EN: There is no line break opportunity between two consecutive characters belonging to the same simple-ruby character complex (cl-22). — JA: 後ろに配置する親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）の文字が，前に配置する親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）と同一の親文字群の文字の場合は，分割不可とする．
cases.rationale: The consequence of membership that a line breaker can be measured on, and the reason the run pairing is data in the input rather than something a runner infers. The group-ruby construct below distributes one run of ruby text across both base characters, so the two occurrences are the same 親文字群 — one simple-ruby character complex — and the quoted first sentence of § C.2 note 7 denies a break between them. The companion case A.22/distinct-complexes/break-and-solid declares the same kind of construct over two base characters with one run each and takes the opposite answer from the same note's second sentence, so the two cases together assert that the distinction is same-run against different-run and not ruby against no-ruby. The expectation states breakability and nothing else on purpose: § B.2 note 10 hands the spacing inside one complex to § 3.3.5 or § 3.3.6, which state where a ruby character sits against its base rather than an amount at this boundary, and Table 1's own cl-22 row and column are published only in the Appendix B PDF that spec/PROVENANCE.toml records and the snapshot deliberately does not carry, so an amount stated here would be invented.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ C.2 note 7, first sentence)

cases.quote: EN: When two adjacent characters belong to two distinct simple-ruby character complex runs, set them solid. ... If two consecutive characters belong to different simple-ruby character complexes (cl-22), a line break opportunity exists between them. — JA: 後ろの文字が前の親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）とは別の親文字群の親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）の場合，その字間はベタ組とする．……別の親文字群の文字の場合は，分割可とする．
cases.rationale: Mono-ruby attaches a run of ruby text to each base character, so the two base characters below are two simple-ruby character complexes and not one, and both notes take their second branch: § B.2 note 10 sets the boundary solid and § C.2 note 7 opens a break. This is why an implementation that models mono-ruby as one complex over the whole compound fails visibly rather than subtly — it forbids the break between two mono-ruby base characters, which is the commonest break opportunity in ruby-annotated Japanese text. `spaces` is empty because solid is what the note says in its own words: this is one of the few cl-22 boundaries whose amount the vendored document actually carries, since Appendix B's tables are published only as PDFs the snapshot does not vendor. One trap is worth naming, because a reader checking this case against the document will meet it: § B.2 note 11's English second sentence is verbatim this note's second sentence and names the simple-ruby complex, while note 11 is about the jukugo-ruby complex and its Japanese half names 熟語ルビ throughout. That is recorded as defect `b2-note-11-simple-ruby-misnomer` in spec/derived/defects.tsv and is carried rather than resolved. This case rests on note 10 and not on note 11.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ B.2 note 10, second sentence; § C.2 note 7, second sentence)

cases.quote: EN: When a simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) or jukugo-ruby character complex (cl-23) is adjacent to katakana (cl-16), the preferred approach is to allow the ruby text to be extended up to the size of the ruby character over the katakana. However, if it is required to conform to JIS X 4051, ruby text shall not be extended over the katakana because katakana characters belong to the ideographic character class in JIS X 4051. There are alternative methods, one of which is to allow ruby text to be extended up to the size of the ruby character over any character including ideographic (cl-19) as well as hiragana (cl-15) and katakana (cl-16) characters, and another is NOT to allow ruby text to be extended over any character from hiragana (cl-15), katakana (cl-16) and ideographic characters (cl-19). — JA: 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22）又は親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ付き）（cl-23）の前又は後ろに片仮名（cl-16），長音記号（cl-10）又は小書きの仮名（cl-11）を配置する場合，ルビ文字を最大でルビ文字の文字サイズまで掛けて配置してよい．ただし，JIS X 4051では，片仮名は，漢字等（cl-19）の文字クラスに含めているので，片仮名にルビ文字を掛けることは禁止されている．なお，平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）だけでなく，漢字等（cl-19）を含めて，すべてルビ文字を最大でルビ文字の文字サイズの1/2まで掛けて配置してよい，とする方法や，平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）及び漢字等（cl-19）のすべてにルビ文字を掛けない，とする処理方法もある．
cases.rationale: The one cl-22 boundary whose amount the document states in words, and the only place all four answers of `ruby.overhang_kana` can be exercised. The ruby text is three characters over a one-character base, so it overflows its base and there is something to hang; the character before the complex is katakana, which both renderings of the note name, so this case does not turn on the divergence spec/derived/defects.tsv records for it — that the Japanese half also names the prolonged sound mark (cl-10) and small kana (cl-11) while the English half names katakana alone. What the case does turn on is the referent and the reading. `ruby_overhang` is the maximum the note permits, not an amount the line realizes: § B.1's legend states the same quantity the same way, 'ruby text can be extended up to the size of the ruby character over the other character', and how much of it a given line uses is § 3.3.8's question. The amount is a fraction of the *ruby* character's em, which is stated by the annotation stream's own `scales` and nowhere else (ADR 0019), so one ruby em is 720 units and resolves to 500 in this case's caller units. The `any` entry is where the two renderings differ and the difference is not recorded anywhere in spec/derived: the English half allows the overhang over every character 'up to the size of the ruby character' while the Japanese half allows it 'up to 1/2 the ruby character size' (最大でルビ文字の文字サイズの1/2まで). spec/derived/questions.tsv selects the Japanese rendering for this question, so the entry below states a half ruby em, and an implementation reading the English half will answer a full one. Under that Japanese reading the answers are not ordered by permissiveness — `any` grants less over a katakana than `kana` does, and buys uniformity across cl-15, cl-16 and cl-19 with it — which is exactly the shape a naive implementation smooths away.

permitted.source: JLReq preferred (§ B.2 note 7, first sentence), which is the answer Policy::JLREQ selects
JLReq preferred (§ B.2 note 7, first sentence), named explicitly
JIS X 4051, as § B.2 note 7's second sentence reports it: katakana is in the ideographic class there and ruby shall not be extended over it
§ B.2 note 7's third sentence, Japanese rendering: a half ruby em over every character, cl-15, cl-16 and cl-19 alike
§ B.2 note 7's third sentence, second alternative: no overhang over hiragana (cl-15), katakana (cl-16) or ideographic characters (cl-19)

disagreements.implementation: CSS Ruby Annotation Layout Module Level 1
disagreements.behavior: Defines `ruby-position`, `ruby-align` and `ruby-merge`, and no property that says how far a ruby annotation may extend over an adjacent character; the `ruby-overhang` property of the earlier CSS3 Ruby draft has no counterpart in Level 1. Whether an annotation overhangs its neighbors, and by how much, is left to the user agent, so a document cannot select any of the four answers § B.2 note 7 lists and two conforming user agents may answer this boundary differently.
disagreements.our_reading: § B.2 note 7 states a preferred answer and three alternatives and does not leave the choice to the formatter. Which one applies is a property of the document's house style, which is why it is a caller-visible question with the Japanese rendering's answer selected, and why this case records all four rather than ours alone. An implementation with no such control is not wrong at this boundary so much as unmeasurable against it, and the report should say which of the four its fixed behavior is closest to.
